sections.title: Clinical Overview & Definitions
sections.content: Distinguishing between Orbital Cellulitis, Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID), and Rhabdomyosarcoma is a hallmark of ophthalmic emergency medicine. Orbital Cellulitis is a life-threatening infection posterior to the orbital septum. IOID (formerly Pseudotumor) is a non-specific, non-granulomatous inflammatory process. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary pediatric orbital malignancy, characterized by aggressive, rapid growth.

sections.title: Chandler Classification of Orbital Infection
content: Stage I: Preseptal Cellulitis (Eyelid edema only)
Stage II: Orbital Cellulitis (Proptosis, chemosis, motility loss)
Stage III: Subperiosteal Abscess (Displacement of globe)
Stage IV: Orbital Abscess (Intra-conal pus collection)
Stage V: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Bilateral signs, CN palsies)

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) — Indicates Compressive Optic Neuropathy
Frozen Orbit (Total Ophthalmoplegia) — Suggests Cavernous Sinus involvement or Apex Syndrome
Rapidly Progressive Proptosis in a Child — Must rule out Rhabdomyosarcoma immediately
Bilateral Orbital Involvement — Consider Systemic Vasculitis, Lymphoma, or Metastasis
Meningismus or Altered Mental Status — Indicates intracranial extension of infection

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Urgent Contrast-Enhanced CT (Orbit/Brain/Sinuses)
2. CBC with Diff, ESR, CRP, Blood Cultures
3. Targeted Biopsy (Mandatory for suspected Rhabdo or non-responsive IOID)
4. Thyroid Function Tests (To rule out TED)
5. c-ANCA / p-ANCA / ACE levels (For GPA or Sarcoidosis)

sections.title: Management: Orbital Cellulitis
content: Admission for IV Antibiotics: Vancomycin (15-20mg/kg) + Ceftriaxone (2g QD)
Add Metronidazole if anaerobic infection suspected (dental origin)
Surgical Drainage if: Vision decreases, APD develops, or no improvement in 48h
Otolaryngology (ENT) consult for sinus debridement
Avoid steroids until 24-48h of antibiotic coverage (and only if improving)

sections.title: Management: IOID (NSOI)
content: High-dose Oral Prednisone: 1mg/kg/day with slow taper
IV Pulse Methylprednisolone for sight-threatening apex cases
Radiation Therapy (1000-3000 cGy) if steroid-resistant or contraindicated
Immunomodulatory Therapy (Steroid-sparing): Methotrexate, Ciclosporin, or Infliximab
Biopsy if atypical or recurrent to rule out Lymphoma

sections.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma Treatment (IRSG)
content: 1. Complete Surgical Excision (only if possible without mutilation)
2. Multi-agent Chemotherapy (VAC: Vincristine, Adriamycin/Actinomycin, Cyclophosphamide)
3. External Beam Radiotherapy (for residual disease)
4. Long-term surveillance for secondary malignancies

content.explanation: B-otryoid (Best), E-mbryonal (Excellent/Common), A-lveolar (Awful/Inferior orbit), M-etastatic (Most concerning)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: In IOID, 'The pain is out of proportion to the clinical signs' initially.
In Cellulitis, always check for 'Pain on eye movement' – it's the most sensitive sign to differentiate from preseptal.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is a 'Great Mimicker' and may present with bruising that looks like trauma.
Wait 24 hours after starting steroids in IOID; if no response, RE-THINK the diagnosis and biopsy.
Orbital Apex Syndrome = CN II, III, IV, V1, VI involvement; localized IOID or aggressive infection.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: IRSG
sections.content: The Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group (IRSG) trials established that orbital rhabdomyosarcoma has a significantly better prognosis than other sites. Modern protocols emphasize globe-sparing treatment with combined chemotherapy and radiation rather than primary exenteration.
